title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
description: Brute force to optimized: extending each rectangle rightward with a running minimum height versus a monotonic increasing stack resolving every bar at once.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given an array of integers heights representing a histogram's bar heights (each bar has width 1, placed side by side), find the area of the LARGEST rectangle that can be formed within the histogram's outline.

blocks.caption: A monotonic increasing stack of bar indices resolves each bar's maximal rectangle the moment a shorter bar arrives, bounding it on both sides

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An array of non-negative integers, each representing one histogram bar's height"],["Output","The area of the largest axis-aligned rectangle fitting entirely within the histogram"],["Goal","Find the maximum rectangle area in a single linear pass"],["Constraints","1 <= heights.length <= 10^5; 0 <= heights[i] <= 10^4"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A rectangle's height is limited by the SHORTEST bar it spans, and it wants to extend as WIDE as possible","For each bar, its maximal possible rectangle is bounded by the nearest SHORTER bar on each side, a classic \"next smaller element\" query"],["Need the answer for EVERY bar (as a potential limiting height) simultaneously","A monotonic stack resolves every bar's left and right boundary in a single linear pass, rather than searching separately for each one"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

For any bar treated as the SHORTEST bar in some rectangle, that rectangle can extend left and right until it hits a bar SHORTER than it (since a shorter bar would break the rectangle's height); finding, for every bar, exactly how far it can extend on both sides gives that bar's maximal possible rectangle area, and the overall answer is the largest such area across all bars.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Widest Possible Fence Panel of a Fixed Height
blocks.text: Imagine a row of fence posts of varying heights, and wanting to attach the largest rectangular panel (of any single height) that fits without sticking out past any post it spans. For a chosen height, the panel can extend left and right only until it reaches a post SHORTER than that height, since the panel cannot extend past a gap where the fence dips below its own height. Checking this for every post's own height (as the panel's height) and taking the best result finds the truly largest possible panel.

blocks.caption: When a shorter bar arrives, every taller bar still on the stack has its rectangle fully bounded: the popped bar's width extends from just after the new top to just before the current position

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: heights = [2,1,5,6,2,3]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Bar (height)","Maximal rectangle","Area","Why"],"rows":[["Index 2 (5)","Spans indices 2-3 (bounded by index 1's height 1 on the left, index 4's height 2 on the right)","5*2=10","Both neighbors are shorter, limiting the rectangle to just these two bars"],["Index 3 (6)","Spans just index 3 (bounded by index 2's height 5 on the left, index 4's height 2 on the right)","6*1=6","The tallest bar, but confined to width 1"],["Answer","10","The largest rectangle found across all bars"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before checking, for every possible starting bar, how far a rectangle can extend rightward (an O(n^2) approach), notice that a monotonic increasing stack resolves EVERY bar's maximal rectangle simultaneously, since a shorter bar arriving is exactly the signal that a taller bar's rectangle can no longer grow.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For bar i to be the SHORTEST (limiting) bar of a rectangle, that rectangle can extend left until hitting the nearest bar strictly SHORTER than heights[i], and right until hitting the nearest bar (strictly or non-strictly, with careful tie-handling) shorter as well.

Observation 2: Walking left to right, maintaining a stack of bar indices with INCREASING heights (bottom to top): whenever a new, SHORTER bar arrives, every taller bar still on the stack has just found its RIGHT boundary (the current position), since nothing beyond this point can be part of THEIR rectangle anymore.

Observation 3: That popped bar's LEFT boundary is whatever is now exposed as the new stack top (or the very beginning, if the stack becomes empty), since that is the nearest bar to its left that is still shorter than it.

Observation 4: Appending a virtual bar of height 0 at the very end of the array forces every remaining bar still on the stack to be resolved, since a height-0 bar is guaranteed to be shorter than everything.
This is the monotonic increasing stack technique: each bar's maximal rectangle is resolved the moment a shorter bar arrives, bounding it precisely between its nearest shorter neighbors on both sides.
6. Brute Force Solution

For each possible starting bar, extend a rectangle rightward one bar at a time, tracking the minimum height included so far (which limits the rectangle's height), and compute the resulting area at each extension.
Step by step algorithm

items: For each starting index i, extend the rectangle to include index j (starting at i, going rightward), tracking the minimum height seen in [i, j].
At each extension, compute the area (minimum height * current width) and track the overall maximum.

codes.python:
def largest_rectangle_area(heights):
    n = len(heights)
    max_area = 0
    for i in range(n):
        min_height = heights[i]
        for j in range(i, n):                                              # extend the rectangle rightward one bar at a time
            min_height = min(min_height, heights[j])                       # the rectangle's height is limited by the SHORTEST bar included
            max_area = max(max_area, min_height * (j - i + 1))
    return max_area


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(largest_rectangle_area([2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Tracking the running minimum height as the rectangle extends directly reflects that a rectangle's height is limited by its SHORTEST included bar.
Computing the area at every single extension ensures no candidate rectangle is missed.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Correctly finds the largest rectangle, since every possible (start, end) span is directly considered with its true limiting height.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2), checking all O(n^2) spans, each processed in O(1) amortized (incremental minimum tracking).
Space: O(1) extra.
Limitation: O(n^2) does not scale to the problem's constraints (up to 10^5 bars); a monotonic stack resolves every bar's maximal rectangle in a single O(n) pass.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force re-derives each rectangle's limiting height from scratch for every starting point. Instead, maintain a monotonic increasing stack of bar indices. Walk through the bars (plus one virtual height-0 bar at the end): whenever the current bar is shorter than the stack's top, pop and resolve that popped bar's maximal rectangle (height = its own height, width = the gap between its new left neighbor on the stack and the current position), repeating until the stack's top is no longer taller. Push the current index.

Walk i from 0 to n (inclusive), using a virtual height of 0 when i equals n. While the stack is non-empty and heights[stack top] >= the current height, pop and compute: height = heights[popped index]; width = i - (new stack top) - 1, or simply i if the stack is now empty; update the maximum area. Push i.
9. Optimized Solution
Use a monotonic increasing stack of bar indices, resolving each bar's maximal rectangle the moment a shorter (or equal) bar arrives.
Dry run for heights = [2,1,5,6,2,3] (plus a virtual 0 at index 6)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each bar is pushed and popped at most once.
Space: O(n), for the stack in the worst case.
Why This Works

Each bar pushed onto the stack represents "a bar still waiting to find its right boundary." The moment a shorter (or equal) bar arrives, it is guaranteed to be exactly that right boundary for every taller bar currently on top of the stack, since anything even shorter appearing earlier would have already resolved them. The popped bar's left boundary is whatever remains exposed on the stack afterward (the nearest bar still shorter than it), giving the FULL width the popped bar's height could span.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A new bar is taller than the stack's top","Simply pushed, still waiting for its own right boundary"],["A new bar is shorter than (or equal to) the stack's top","The top is popped and resolved: its rectangle spans from just after the new top to just before the current position"],["The virtual height-0 bar at the very end","Guarantees every remaining bar on the stack gets fully resolved, since nothing can be shorter than 0"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The virtual 0-height bar (at index n, beyond the real array) elegantly avoids needing separate cleanup logic after the main loop for bars still on the stack.
The width calculation (i - stack top - 1, or just i if the stack empties) correctly measures the FULL span between the popped bar's two shorter neighbors.
Using >= (not just >) in the popping condition correctly handles equal-height bars, ensuring the widest possible rectangle is found even among ties.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

The classic "largest rectangle in a histogram" problem is solved by a monotonic increasing stack: for every bar, its maximal rectangle is exactly bounded by its nearest strictly shorter neighbors on each side, resolved directly the moment a shorter bar is encountered while scanning.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting the virtual height-0 bar at the end, which would leave bars still on the stack unresolved after the main loop.
Computing the width incorrectly, forgetting to subtract 1 (or mishandling the empty-stack case) when measuring the span between the new stack top and the current position.
Using a strict > instead of >= in the popping condition, which can miss slightly wider rectangles among bars of equal height.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["A single bar","The answer is simply that bar's height (width 1)"],["All bars the same height","The answer is height * n, the full histogram width"],["Strictly increasing or strictly decreasing heights","Still correctly handled: each bar is resolved once a shorter one is encountered (or by the final virtual 0 bar)"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly stating "the virtual 0-height bar at the end avoids needing a separate cleanup pass" up front demonstrates a clean, complete understanding of the technique's edge-case handling.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Largest rectangle bounded by the shortest bar it spans, in a histogram" points directly to the monotonic increasing stack technique.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How does this problem extend to Maximal Rectangle (finding the largest all-1s rectangle in a 2D binary matrix)? Each row of the matrix can be treated as a histogram (accumulating consecutive 1s vertically), and this exact algorithm applied per row solves that 2D variant.

Why does the popping condition use >= rather than just >? Using >= (popping on equal heights too) ensures that when multiple equal-height bars are adjacent, the widest possible span among them is still correctly found rather than missed.
What is the maximum possible stack size during the algorithm? Up to n+1 (including the virtual bar), occurring when heights are in strictly increasing order.

items: The foundational monotonic stack technique directly reused (per-row) in Maximal Rectangle elsewhere in this project's Matrix category, and conceptually related to Trapping Rain Water's boundary-based area calculations.

blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space.
Optimized (monotonic increasing stack): O(n) time, O(n) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Monotonic increasing stack for "largest rectangle bounded by nearest shorter neighbors"

Core Idea: Each bar's maximal rectangle is resolved the moment a shorter bar arrives; its width spans from the nearest shorter bar on the left (now exposed on the stack) to the current position on the right
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: A virtual height-0 bar appended at the end forces every remaining bar on the stack to be resolved, avoiding a separate cleanup pass
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Monotonic increasing stack; a shorter arrival resolves height x (gap between the new top and current position) for everything taller waiting
